procedural_history.impugned_order: Decision dated February 3, 1965, of the Labour Court, Patna, setting aside the order of discharge from service passed by the Appellant-Company against the respondent and directing his reinstatement.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant-Company appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the order of the Labour Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26(2) is confined only to cases of misconduct as defined in Rule 20 of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Rules, 1955.

facts: An employee was discharged by their company for alleged misconduct.
The company argued that the Labour Court lacked jurisdiction to hear the employee's complaint under Section 26(2) of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act, 1953.
The company's central argument was that the specific misconduct alleged was not one of the types listed in Rule 20 of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Rules, 1955.
law: Section 26(1) of the Act requires an employer to give notice before dismissing an employee.
The proviso to Section 26(1) creates an exception, allowing for dismissal without notice for specific misconducts defined in the rules.
Rule 20 lists the specific acts of misconduct that fall under the proviso to Section 26(1).
Section 26(2) of the Act allows a dismissed employee to file a complaint on grounds that, among others, they were not guilty of "any misconduct" or that they were not given the required notice.
application: The Court focused on the plain language of Section 26(2), which allows an employee to complain that they were not guilty of "any misconduct". The Court interpreted the word "any" broadly, concluding it is not restricted to the specific misconducts listed in Rule 20.

The Court clarified the limited purpose of Rule 20. It determined that Rule 20's sole function is to specify the types of misconduct for which an employer can dismiss an employee without the notice required by Section 26(1). It does not define the entire universe of misconduct for which an employee can be dismissed or for which a complaint can be filed.

The Court identified a logical flaw in the company's argument. Section 26(2) explicitly allows an employee to complain that "no notice was served as required by sub-sec. 1". If the Labour Court's jurisdiction were limited to Rule 20 misconducts (where no notice is required), this ground for complaint would be superfluous and meaningless.

The presence of the 'no notice' ground in Section 26(2) makes it "abundantly clear" that the subsection applies to all cases of dismissal and discharge, not just those falling under the Rule 20 proviso.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26(2) is not confined to cases of misconduct defined in Rule 20. The Court reasoned that the plain language of the statute, particularly the phrase "any misconduct" and the inclusion of a ground for complaint based on lack of notice, demonstrates that the section applies to all types of dismissals, not just those specified in the rules for dispensing with notice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26 is a limited one, similar to that under Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, allowing interference with a domestic enquiry only on grounds of perversity or breach of natural justice.

facts: An argument was made that the Labour Court's jurisdiction under Section 26 of the Bihar Shops and Establishment Act is limited.
This argument sought to equate the jurisdiction under Section 26 with the more restrictive jurisdiction under Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
Under this limited view, the Labour Court could only interfere with a domestic enquiry's findings on grounds of perversity, breach of natural justice, victimisation, or unfair labour practice.
law: Section 26(2) and (5) of the Bihar Shops and Establishment Act outlines the procedure for complaints against dismissal.
Under Section 26, an employee has the right to show that there was no reasonable cause for their dismissal or that they were not guilty of the alleged misconduct.
The Court noted that the purposes and language of Section 26 of the Act and Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act are different and not comparable.
application: The Supreme Court found the argument to be contrary to the express language of Section 26.
It clarified that proceedings under Section 26 are not an appeal against a domestic enquiry. Instead, they are "independent and original proceedings."
In these original proceedings, the Labour Court is required to record its own evidence and arrive at its "own findings" based on that evidence, irrespective of the findings from the domestic enquiry.

The fact that an employee can argue they were not guilty of misconduct demonstrates that the Labour Court must assess the evidence on its own merits, not just review the procedure of the prior enquiry.
Therefore, the Court's role is not a limited review for procedural flaws (like under Section 33A), but a full, independent adjudication of the complaint.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26 is not a limited one. It is an independent and original jurisdiction where the court must record its own evidence and come to its own findings, rather than simply reviewing the domestic enquiry for perversity or procedural errors.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26(2) is confined only to cases of misconduct as defined in Rule 20 of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Rules, 1955.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's counsel argued that a complaint can be filed with the Labour Court only if the misconduct is one of those specifically set out in Rule 20.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's position, as upheld by the court, was that the jurisdiction is not limited by Rule 20. The rule's proviso only serves to dispense with the notice requirement in certain cases of misconduct, but does not restrict the types of complaints that can be filed under the main sections of the Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26 is a limited one, similar to that under Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, allowing interference with a domestic enquiry only on grounds of perversity or breach of natural justice.
appellant_arguments: The appellant (the Company) contended that its order was a 'discharge simpliciter' due to a loss of trust and confidence, not a punishment, and therefore the Labour Court had no jurisdiction. It also argued that the Labour Court's findings were perverse, implying that the court's review should be limited to such grounds and it should not re-evaluate the merits of the company's decision.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's complaint alleged that the company's officers acted in collusion and used 'threat and undue influence,' inviting a full factual inquiry by the Labour Court. The respondent's position, as evidenced by the Labour Court's actions, was that the court had the power to go into the merits of the case, re-appreciate the evidence, and determine if the termination was justified, not just review the domestic enquiry for procedural flaws.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A complaint filed by an employee under Section 26(2) is not limited to cases of misconduct specified in Rule 20. The term "any misconduct" in sub-section 2 encompasses all forms of misconduct, and the proviso in sub-section 1 only serves to dispense with the notice requirement for misconducts listed in the rules, without restricting the overall scope of sub-section 2. Consequently, the competent authority has the jurisdiction to hear the complaint, record evidence, and make its own findings on the matter.
obiter: There is no comparison between Section 26 of the Act and Section 33A of the Industrial Disputes Act, as the purposes of the two sections are different.
In an appeal under Article 136, the Supreme Court will not go behind a finding of fact unless it is perverse or unreasonable.
A judicial decision is not of assistance as precedent if it contains hardly any reasoning or if the statutory provisions it deals with are not in pari materia with the statute in question.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The jurisdiction of the Labour Court under Section 26 of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act is broad and not confined to the specific misconducts listed in Rule 20. The statute empowers the Labour Court to conduct its own inquiry, record evidence, and come to its own findings on the merits of a dismissal or discharge, irrespective of the findings of any domestic enquiry conducted by the employer.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory interpretation based on the 'clear language' of Section 26, sub-sections (1), (2), and (5) of the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that jurisdiction is confined to misconducts in Rule 20 was rejected because the 'clear language' of the statute does not support it. The court reasoned that the proviso in sub-section (1) concerning Rule 20 only serves to 'dispense with notice' in those specific cases, not to limit the types of complaints that can be filed.
The court pointed to the words 'any misconduct' in sub-section (2) to show that the right to complain is not confined to the misconducts listed in Rule 20.

The appellant's argument that the termination was a 'discharge simpliciter' was found to be 'inconsistent with the record before us and is manifestly untenable.' The court noted that the charge-sheet, the enquiry findings, the discharge order itself, and the company's own written statement before the Labour Court all explicitly referred to the action as a 'punishment' for 'misconduct'.

The argument that the Labour Court's jurisdiction was limited to reviewing the domestic enquiry for perversity was rejected, as the court affirmed the Labour Court's power under Section 26(5) to 'record evidence and come to its own findings irrespective of the findings of the domestic enquiry'.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position that the Labour Court's jurisdiction was not limited by Rule 20 was upheld because the court's interpretation of the 'clear language' of Section 26(2) showed that the words 'any misconduct' apply to all cases of dismissal and discharge.

The court's interpretation of Section 26(2) also found that if the appellant's view were correct, the ground for complaint that 'no notice was served' would be superfluous, which strengthened the respondent's case for a broader reading of the statute.

The respondent's position that the Labour Court could conduct a full factual inquiry was affirmed by the court's reading of Section 26(5), which empowers the authority to record evidence, hear parties, make its own inquiry, and pass reasoned orders, including reinstatement or compensation.
